recipe.history:
Long before Paul McCartney penned the 1973 Wings anthem "Band on the Run" — that restless, soaring ode to escape and reinvention — the humble hamburger bun was quietly staging its own great escape from obscurity. The soft, enriched bread roll we now take for granted as the burger's inseparable companion has its roots in the wave of German immigration to the American Midwest in the mid-nineteenth century. Bakers brought with them the tradition of the Rundstück, a small, round, slightly sweet roll made with milk, butter, and egg — a far cry from the dense rye loaves of the old country, and perfectly suited to the new world's appetite for something tender, yielding, and fast. Early hamburger vendors at county fairs and lunch counters in cities like Hamburg, New York, and Cincinnati placed their loose beef patties between slices of ordinary sandwich bread, but it was the soft roll that would ultimately win the battle for the burger's soul.

By the early twentieth century, the bun had ceased to be a mere vessel and had become a co-star. When White Castle standardized the slider and its diminutive steamed bun in 1921, they weren't just solving a logistics problem — they were making a philosophical statement: the bread and the beef are a unit, inseparable, each one elevated by the other. The bun's crumb must be open enough to absorb the fat and juices of the patty without collapsing into a sodden mass, yet structured enough to hold its shape through the final, glorious bite. A good bun is toasted on the cut face until just golden, so that a thin crust forms — a barricade against the inevitable flood of rendered beef fat, melted cheese, and condiment — while the outer dome stays pillowy and soft against the palm of your hand. Getting that balance right is as much an act of craft as any riff McCartney ever played.

I remember the first time a burger bun genuinely stopped me in my tracks. I was maybe eleven years old, standing at a cookout in my uncle's backyard in central New Jersey, the kind of late-August afternoon where the air smells like cut grass and lighter fluid and the particular promise of something great about to happen. My uncle pulled a tray of homemade brioche buns from the oven — golden, shiny with egg wash, their tops split just slightly where the dough had bloomed — and I remember thinking they looked more like something from a bakery window than from a suburban kitchen. He sliced them, pressed the cut faces down onto the griddle beside the patties, and in thirty seconds they were transformed: caramelized, fragrant, with a surface that crackled faintly when you pressed it with a finger. That burger, whatever was on it, was the best I had ever eaten. It wasn't the patty that made it. It was the bun.

There is a school of thought that insists a burger must be cooked through — that anything pink in the center is a liability, a risk not worth taking. I reject this entirely, and I reject it with feeling. Medium rare, that narrow band between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit, is where beef lives. It is where the myoglobin is still pink and the muscle fibers have contracted just enough to push fat and juice toward the surface without squeezing them out entirely. The crust is hard and deeply browned from the Maillard reaction, the interior is warm and yielding, and when you bite through it there is a give — a slight resistance followed by a clean release — that is one of the most satisfying textures in all of food. To cook a burger beyond this point is to chase the moisture and the flavor out of the meat and into the fire. The bun deserves better. The beef deserves better. Paul McCartney, were he to weigh in, would almost certainly agree.
ingredients: 300g (2½ cups) bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
115g (½ cup / 1 stick) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
680g (1½ lbs) freshly ground beef, 80/20 chuck-to-fat ratio
3 large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced
4 large shallots, peeled and sliced into thin rings
Neutral oil (e.g. canola or vegetable), for frying
4 leaves green leaf lettuce, washed and dried
2 large heirloom tomatoes, sliced ¼-inch thick
1 ripe avocado, halved, pitted, and sliced
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE (or at least 5 hours ahead): In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine the bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Whisk briefly to distribute. Add the 2 eggs and warm milk. Mix on low speed for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms, then increase to medium and knead for 5 minutes.

2. With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one or two cubes at a time, waiting until each addition is fully incorporated before adding the next. This will take 8–10 minutes. The dough will look broken and greasy at first — keep going. It should eventually become smooth, glossy, and pull away from the sides of the bowl cleanly.
3. Transfer the dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) or for at least 4 hours. Cold dough is far easier to shape and develops better flavor.

4. Turn the cold dough out onto a lightly floured surface and divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 150g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Flatten each ball gently with your palm to a disc about 1 inch tall.
5. Cover loosely with oiled plastic wrap and proof at room temperature until puffy and nearly doubled, about 1.5–2 hours.

6. Preheat the oven to 375°F / 190°C. Whisk together the remaining egg and heavy cream to make the egg wash. Brush the top and sides of each bun generously. Sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake for 16–18 minutes, rotating the pan halfway, until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

7. MAKE THE CARAMELIZED ONION JAM: In a wide, heavy-bottomed skillet or Dutch oven, melt the butter with the olive oil over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and salt. Stir to coat. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring every 5–8 minutes, for 45–55 minutes total. The onions will wilt, then steam, then slowly brown. Do not rush this with high heat.

8. When the onions are deeply golden and jammy, add the brown sugar, balsamic vinegar, and thyme. Stir and cook for another 5–8 minutes until most of the liquid has evaporated and the mixture is thick and glossy. Taste and adjust seasoning. Set aside. Can be made up to 3 days ahead and refrigerated.

9. MAKE THE SMASH SAUCE: Combine the mayonnaise, mustard, ketchup, pickle brine, hot sauce, smoked paprika, onion powder, and cayenne in a small bowl. Whisk until smooth. Taste and adjust. Refrigerate until needed.

10. MAKE THE CRISPY SHALLOTS: Place the sliced shallots in a bowl, pour the buttermilk over them, and let soak for at least 20 minutes. In a separate wide bowl, whisk together the flour, salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Pour 2–3 inches of neutral oil into a heavy pot and heat to 350°F / 175°C.

11. Working in batches, lift the shallots from the buttermilk (letting the excess drip off) and toss them in the seasoned flour, pressing gently to adhere. Shake off excess flour and fry for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Transfer to a paper towel-lined plate and season immediately with a pinch of flaky salt. Keep warm.

12. MAKE THE MAPLE PEPPER BACON: Preheat the oven to 400°F / 205°C. Lay the bacon strips on a wire rack set over a foil-lined baking sheet. Brush the tops with maple syrup and sprinkle with cracked pepper. Bake for 16–20 minutes until caramelized and crisp but not brittle. Drain briefly on paper towels.

13. FORM AND SEASON THE PATTIES: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g / 6 oz each). Handle the meat as little as possible — overworking it produces a dense, tough burger. Gently form each portion into a loosely packed disc about ¾ inch thick, wider than you think you need (they will shrink). Make a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming. Season both sides generously with flaky salt and cracked black pepper just before cooking.

14. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place the patties in the pan without crowding — cook in batches if needed. Do not press. Sear for 3–3.5 minutes on the first side without moving, until a deep brown crust has formed.

15. Flip once. Immediately lay one slice of aged cheddar and one slice of American cheese on each patty. Cook for 2–2.5 minutes on the second side. Use an instant-read thermometer to check: you are aiming for 130–135°F / 54–57°C at the thickest point. Pull the patties from the heat at this temperature — residual heat will carry them a few degrees further. Rest for 2 minutes.

16. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice the brioche buns in half. Spread a thin layer of unsalted butter on the cut faces. Place cut-side down on the same hot skillet or griddle for 60–90 seconds until golden with lightly crisped edges. Watch carefully — brioche's sugar content means it colors quickly.

17. ASSEMBLE: Spread a generous tablespoon of smash sauce on both cut faces of each toasted bun. On the bottom bun, layer: a leaf of green leaf lettuce, 2 slices of heirloom tomato (seasoned with a pinch of flaky salt), 4 bread-and-butter pickle chips, and several slices of avocado.

18. Place the double-cheesed medium-rare patty directly on top of the avocado. Spoon 2 tablespoons of caramelized onion jam over the melted cheese. Lay 2 strips of maple-pepper bacon across the jam, breaking them to fit if needed. Crown with a generous tangle of crispy shallots.
19. Cap with the top bun, press gently, and serve immediately. Internal temperature at service should be 130–135°F / 54–57°C — pink, juicy, and exactly as nature and Paul McCartney intended.
